title: Body of missing painter found floating in his flooded house verandah
text:
Kanpur: The body of a 32-year-old painter missing for two days, was found floating in the flooded verandah of his house in Ujiyarpurwa, Kanpur on Thursday morning. Police suspect he was electrocuted and have sent the body for a post-mortem examination.
Sanjay alias Lala had lived with his mother, Tara Devi, for about 10 years in landlord Shyambabu alias Pajiâs house. He was alone after his mother moved to a relativeâs home in Lalbangla because of flooding.
The landlord said flood conditions had persisted in Ujiyarpurwa for about 15 days, submerging hundreds of houses and forcing residents to live on rooftops.
After Sanjay had not been seen for two days, the landlord made inquiries with his married sisters, Mona and Preeti, but found no information. He also searched the flooded lower portion of the house but could not locate him. Preetiâs husband, Shekhar, was then informed, while calls to Sanjayâs mobile phone found it switched off.
At about 6.30am on Thursday, family members and the landlord found Sanjayâs body floating in water in the lower veranda and alerted Nawabganj police.
Police struggled to reach the house because of the high water level. They reached the area with a loader, recovered the body and sent it for a post-mortem examination.
Nawabganj inspector Rajkesar said Sanjayâs body was found in floodwater inside the house and that electrocution was suspected. Family members believe he may have come into contact with electric current while fixing wires in the room. Investigation is underway.

title: Ganesh idol-makers face losses as flood-hit people scale down, cancel celebrations
text:
Kendrapada:
 Idol makers in Kendrapada and Jajpur districts are staring at huge losses following cancellation or scaling down of Ganesh Puja celebrations in several flood-hit educational institutions and public places. The floodwaters are yet to completely recede from several riverside villages in Aul, Rajkanika, Pattamundai and Rajnagar blocks of Kendrapada district and Dasarathpur, Bari, Binjharpur, Barachana and Rasulpur blocks of Jajpur district.
Idol makers said they usually receive orders from educational institutions nearly a month before Ganesh Puja. âBut the recent floods have washed away our hopes of earning more this year, as many institutions will not celebrate Ganesh Puja with enthusiasm. Several puja committees in flood-hit areas have decided to skip the festival,â said Pravat Behera (63), an idol maker from Kumbhara Sahi, on the outskirts of town. Narendra Moharana (40), an idol-maker from Parakula village, said our business is facing 50% losses due to the flood.
Idol makers in Jajpur district have been badly affected too. âThe recent flood has severely hit our work and with it our business. We are in great distress,â said Pramod Behera (54), an idol maker from Balichandrapur.
âUsually, by this time, we receive orders from Ganesh Puja organisers. However, many organisers have decided not to observe the puja this year because of the flood. We have been making idols for generations, but we have never faced such a scenario,â said Basant Behera of Kumbharasahi, Kendrapada.
Impact of the flood has also dampened the festive spirit among people. Sahadev Mallick (45) of Kaspa village in Jajpur districtâs Dasarathpur block said the Kani river breached the village about two weeks ago, leaving the entire area marooned.
Students in flood-hit schools said the celebrations would be subdued this year. âWe used to celebrate Ganesh Puja in a big way. But the school was submerged in floodwater and muddy water is still visible inside classrooms,â said Rajesh Das (12), a Class VI student of Malikapur School in the worst-affected Malikapur village under Dasarathpur block.
Similarly, students of Padanipala village under Aul block said their school had remained submerged for nearly a month, forcing them to cancel the celebrations. âEvery year we celebrate Ganesh Puja. But uncertainty is now haunting us as the government has failed to provide us relief,â said Bichitrananda Das (13), a Class VII student of a high school in Padanipala.
Residents of other flood-hit villages also said their immediate priority was rebuilding their lives rather than celebrating the festival. âHow can we celebrate? There is nothing left here except damaged houses,â said Parikhita Jena of Singhgaon village under Pattamundai block.

title: Govt seeks data on flood-hit schools, damage
text:
Patna:
 The education department has sought a consolidated report from all district education officers (DEOs) on schools affected by the ongoing floods and damage to school buildings, educational materials and other infrastructure.
During a video conference on Tuesday, education department special secretary 
Dharmendra Kumar
 directed all DEOs to submit updated data on flood-affected schools in their respective districts.
The department also directed officials to ensure that the education of children staying in relief camps is not disrupted due to the closure of their schools. Teachers from schools shut because of flood, whose students are staying in relief camps, have been asked to be deputed to the camps to continue classes.
Officials were also directed to submit detailed reports. The department stressed that the data should be accurate and updated to help the govt assess the situation and take appropriate measures.

title: Nepal floods: Survivor captures horrifying moment flash floods engulf homes, roads and buildings
text:
NEW DELHI: A new video from Nepal appears to capture the terrifying moments as flash floodwaters surge through a settlement, sweeping away houses, buildings and parts of a road while people scramble for higher ground. Students can be seen inside what appears to be a school building as the water level of a nearby river rises rapidly.
The footage was uploaded on the Facebook page of Nepal7 media outlet and appears to have been recorded from inside a school, where several students are initially seen. Within minutes, floodwaters surge through a stream close to the building, carrying boulders, debris and water, while nearby buildings and a road on which vehicles had been travelling appear to be swept away and submerged. As the torrent intensifies, the person recording the footage and the students move up the stairs inside the building to reach higher ground.
The video comes as Nepal continues to deal with the aftermath of devastating flash floods that authorities said had killed 1,356 people by Monday.
According to Nepalâs National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), rescue teams were still searching for 4,996 people, including at least 589 foreign nationals. 
Around 13,400 people had been rescued.
The floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, according to authorities. The resulting surge travelled downstream through the Bhotekoshi River, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.
The disaster also affected neighbouring Tibet and China. Chinese media reports said at least 43 people were killed on the Chinese side, while more than 500 remained missing in Tibet.
NDRRMA said 363 bodies had been recovered in Chitwan, 223 in Nawalparasi East, 221 in Nawalparasi West, 197 in Nuwakot, 169 in Rasuwa, 75 in Gorkha, 70 in Dhading and 38 in Tanahu.
Identifying the dead has remained a major challenge. Only 98 bodies had been identified and handed over to families by Monday, according to NDRRMA. Nepal Police has been collecting DNA samples from relatives of missing people to help identify unclaimed remains.
More than 1,000 unidentified bodies have been buried after DNA samples were collected for future identification, officials said.
Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, marking the continuing toll of the disaster.

title: Nepal’s flood bill could hit $5 billion. Where will the money come from?
text:
It's been more than 10 days since a glacial collapse sent freezing water, rocks and debris roaring down Nepal's Bhotekoshi and Trishuli valleys.
The death toll has risen to 1,357, while 5,326 people remain missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Rescue teams have so far saved 13,583 people.
The disaster has also inflicted an enormous economic cost. Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority estimates that the floods caused NPR 387.54 billion ($2.56 billion) in damage to property, housing and infrastructure. The government says its immediate four-month recovery effort will require another NPR 7.95 billion, or about $53 million, for roads, temporary shelters, drinking water and electricity.
The tragedy has let to tohusands being killed while over 5,000 are missing
But that is only the beginning.
Nepal's finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters that the eventual reconstruction bill could reach $4 billion to $5 billion, roughly a tenth of Nepal's annual economic output. The figure remains preliminary and could change as authorities complete detailed assessments.
For a country with an economy of about $46 billion, the scale of the challenge is daunting.
Nepal is not entering the crisis with unlimited fiscal room. 
It is still dealing with the legacy of the 2015 earthquake, while public debt has risen sharply over the past decade.
The question now is simple but difficult: Where will the money to rebuild come from?
A tight fiscal position
Nepal's government will have to shoulder part of the cost itself.
It can reprioritise spending, use existing disaster-response resources and increase borrowing. But each option comes with a price.
The IMF estimates Nepal's public debt at 49.6% of GDP in FY2025-26, up from 48.1% a year earlier. It also expects the country to continue running a fiscal deficit as the government seeks to increase revenue and improve public-investment execution.
A large reconstruction programme would therefore compete with spending on schools, hospitals, jobs and other infrastructure.
Borrowing could help bridge part of the gap, but greater reliance on debt would increase future debt-servicing costs and leave less room for development spending.
Nepal therefore needs not just money, but financing that can be mobilised quickly and channelled into reconstruction projects.
An economy already under strain
The disaster has hit sectors that Nepal has been relying on to strengthen its economy.
Remittances remain the country's biggest external financial cushion. The IMF expects workers' remittances to reach $15.2 billion in FY2025-26, equivalent to 33.1 per cent of GDP.
But remittances are household income, not government revenue. They support consumption and provide foreign exchange, but Kathmandu cannot simply redirect that money towards rebuilding public infrastructure.
That makes sectors such as hydropower and tourism especially important to the recovery.
Hydropower has been one of Nepal's biggest growth opportunities, with the country seeking to harness its Himalayan rivers to generate electricity and expand exports to India. But at least 11 hydropower projects in the affected corridor have been damaged, knocking generating capacity offline.
Tourism faces a different risk. Nepal's trekking, mountaineering and pilgrimage industries depend heavily on access to mountain regions. Damaged roads and bridges could therefore disrupt visitor flows and hurt another important source of foreign exchange.
Nepal now has to rebuild while some of the very sectors expected to drive future growth have themselves taken a hit.
Domestic financing: The first layer
The first layer of the reconstruction effort will come from Nepal's own resources.
The government can reprioritise its budget, divert spending towards damaged infrastructure and draw on disaster-response funds. It can also increase domestic or external borrowing.
But these resources will not be enough on their own.
The government will have to decide what gets rebuilt first. Roads and bridges reconnecting isolated communities, electricity infrastructure and housing for displaced families are likely to take priority over projects that can wait.
Nepal's own resources will therefore form the foundation of the financing package, rather than cover the entire reconstruction bill.
Insurance and private capital
Commercial assets provide another, albeit more limited, source of funding.
Hydropower projects and other insured businesses can receive payouts for physical damage and, in some cases, business interruption.
Nepal's Insurance Authority had received 583 flood-related claims worth NPR 25.87 billion ($171 million) as of August 31. The figure represents reported claims and insured exposure rather than final payouts, with assessments still under way.
Hydropower projects are expected to account for a significant share of those claims, given the concentration of damage along the affected river corridors.
Insurance payouts could help companies repair or replace damaged assets, but they cannot finance public infrastructure such as roads, bridges and settlements.
Private investment could provide another source of capital, particularly for hydropower. Companies can raise equity, borrow against future electricity revenues and use insurance proceeds to restore damaged facilities.
But private capital has a natural limit.
An investor can finance a power plant because it can sell electricity and generate a return. There is far less incentive to finance a remote road or bridge that provides a public benefit but generates no direct revenue.
Public infrastructure will therefore continue to depend heavily on government and donor financing.
Development banks: The biggest external pool
The largest external financing pool is likely to come from international development institutions.
The UN and humanitarian partners have already appealed for $49.6 million to help more than 84,000 people with food, shelter, healthcare, clean water and cash assistance over four months. The Asian Development Bank has separately approved a $5 million emergency grant.
But these are emergency funds, not long-term reconstruction financing.
For the rebuilding phase, Kathmandu can turn to institutions such as the World Bank and ADB for concessional loans, grants and project financing.
Nepal already has a disaster-financing mechanism with the World Bank. In 2024, the bank approved $150 million in contingent financing under a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option, allowing the government to access funds after a qualifying natural disaster.
Such instruments can provide immediate liquidity. But a reconstruction programme running into several billion dollars would require fresh commitments from multilateral lenders, bilateral donors and other development partners.
Bilateral aid
Nepal is also receiving assistance directly from other countries, although most of it so far has focused on emergency relief and rescue rather than long-term reconstruction.
The UK has offered Â£5 million ($6.8 million) in aid, while South Korea has pledged $1 million in humanitarian assistance. The US initially committed $500,000 and later increased its contribution to $3.6 million for food and emergency supplies.
India has provided relief supplies, rescue personnel and technical assistance, including more than 68 tonnes of relief material.
India hap launched special helplines for Indians seeking information
Nepal's foreign ministry says it has received support from a wider group of countries, including Japan, Australia, Germany, Qatar, the UAE, China and Canada. It has also said Nepal has received monetary pledges from international partners, although the government has not published a consolidated country-by-country tally as of now.
These contributions are significant for the immediate response. But the next phase will require something much larger: bilateral grants, concessional financing and project-specific support for reconstruction.
For Kathmandu, grants would be particularly valuable because they would not add to its debt burden. But bilateral aid alone cannot close the financing gap.
Climate finance: Another potential source
Another potential source of funding is the international "loss and damage" fund, created after years of demands from vulnerable developing countries that they should receive financial support for climate-related destruction they did little to cause.
The fund was agreed at the UN climate summit in Egypt in 2022 and formally operationalised at COP28 in Dubai in 2023. At COP28, countries agreed that the World Bank would host the fund temporarily and administer it as a financial intermediary.
Governments contribute to the fund, but those contributions are voluntary rather than a mandatory bill imposed on particular countries. More than $720 million had been pledged by COP29 in 2024.
Nepal is now seeking access to that money. Its foreign minister has called for $20 million from the loss-and-damage mechanism following the floods, arguing that Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse-gas emissions while facing severe climate risks.
However, $20 million would cover only a tiny fraction of a potential $4 billion-$5 billion reconstruction bill.
The loss-and-damage fund can therefore provide an additional source of financing, but it is unlikely to come close to funding Nepal's entire recovery.
The government is also turning to Parliament to assess in more specific terms how the disaster could affect Nepalâs economy and how it can tap climate finance. A seven-member Finance Committee sub-panel, formed on Wednesday (September 9), has been asked to study the economic impact of the August 26 floods and issues related to climate finance, with its report due by September 18.
The 2015 earthquake offers a blueprint
Nepal has a precedent for financing reconstruction on a multibillion-dollar scale.
The 2015 earthquake caused around $7 billion in physical damage and generated reconstruction needs estimated at roughly $6.7 billion.
At an international conference that year, donors and development partners pledged about $4.1 billion for Nepal's reconstruction. The World Bank alone committed up to $500 million.
That experience offers the clearest indication of what a financing package for the current disaster could look like.
Nepal would put some of its own resources into reconstruction, while development partners provide grants and concessional loans and private investors finance commercially viable projects.
But there is one major difference: Nepal now has a much larger debt burden than it did before the 2015 earthquake.
That makes the terms of external financing particularly important. Grants and highly concessional loans would place significantly less pressure on government finances than commercial borrowing.
The cost that cannot be counted
Nepal is therefore facing a financing stack rather than a single source of money.
The scale of the destruction means these sources will have to be combined and coordinated. To avoid substantially increasing its debt burden, Kathmandu will need a much larger international financing package, including grants and other assistance that does not have to be repaid, alongside concessional loans and other forms of financing.
Even then, the $4 billion-$5 billion reconstruction estimate will not capture every cost.
The economic loss from thousands of deaths and missing people, for instance, extends far beyond the value of damaged property and infrastructure. Families can lose their main source of income when a breadwinner dies, while survivors may face injuries, displacement, interrupted work and psychological trauma.
Children may lose schooling. Businesses may lose workers and customers.
These losses are much harder to quantify than a damaged road or power plant, but they can prolong the economic impact of the disaster for years.
How the disaster happened
The resilience question
There is one more complication: the final bill could rise if Nepal decides to rebuild differently.
Replacing a bridge with another bridge in the same vulnerable location may restore a transport link quickly, but it does little to reduce the risk of another disaster.
The World Bank estimates that Nepal needs $47.4 billion in adaptation investment between 2021 and 2050. That figure covers the country's much broader climate-adaptation requirements and should not be confused with the current flood reconstruction bill.
For Kathmandu, rebuilding presents a fundamental choice: replace damaged infrastructure as quickly and cheaply as possible, or spend more to make it more resilient.
The second option may require greater upfront investment, but it could reduce the cost of future disasters.
That choice is also likely to shape Nepal's international financing appeal. Donors and development banks have increasingly linked reconstruction funding to resilience, disaster-risk reduction and climate adaptation.
For now, Nepal's immediate challenge is to finance a potential $5 billion reconstruction bill.
Its bigger challenge is to ensure that the money does not simply rebuild what the floods destroyed, but helps build infrastructure capable of withstanding what comes next.

title: Watch: Floods rock Japan's Nagoya as streets turn into sea, manhole explodes
text:
Nagoya, a city in Japan in began assessing the damage from record rainfall on Wednesday after Japanâs highest-level flood warning for the Shonai River was lowered overnight and evacuation instructions were withdrawn. Nagoya City said the Disaster Relief Act had been applied across the city from September 8, opening the way for emergency assistance in areas affected by the flooding.
The first official damage assessment released by the Aichi Prefectural Government on Wednesday reported three minor injuries â one in Nagoya and two in Kitanagoya. One house was partially damaged, while 16 homes were flooded above floor level and 27 below it. About 200 vehicles in Nagoya were also reported flooded and unable to move.
The immediate river threat eased during the early hours of Wednesday. The Level 5 flood warning for the Shonai River was lowered to a Level 2 advisory at 12.40am, according to Jiji Press. Nagoya City separately said it withdrew a Level 4 evacuation instruction for the Yada River at 2.45am after conditions fell below the relevant threshold.
Nagoya is the capital of Aichi prefecture in central Japan and home to about 2.35 million people, according to city data. 
The city is a major transport and industrial centre in the Tokai region.
Record rain hits Nagoya
The emergency followed an exceptional spell of rain on Tuesday.
Japan Meteorological Agency data show Nagoya received 104.5mm of rain in one hour on September 8, the highest hourly total recorded at the station since observations began in 1890. The previous record was 97mm, set in September 2000. Nagoya received 219.5mm of rain over the day, according to JMA.
A video posted by the X account GlobeUpdate purports to show flooding in Nagoya during Tuesdayâs downpour. The post cites the 104.5mm hourly rainfall figure, which matches JMA data.
Heavy rain repeatedly hit Aichi and neighbouring Gifu prefecture as developed rain clouds passed over the same areas. Roads were inundated and transport was disrupted across Nagoya.
Nagoya City said bus and subway services were affected and temporary refuge facilities were opened for people unable to return home after public transport was disrupted.
The Associated Press reported that about 3,500 people sought shelter during the flooding.
Highest flood warning issued
As conditions deteriorated on Tuesday evening, Japanese meteorological and river authorities issued a Level 5 flood warning for the Shonai River.
The Japan Meteorological Agency said the warning was issued on September 8 after the river reached conditions indicating an extremely high likelihood that a disaster had already occurred in designated flood-risk areas.
Level 5 is the highest category in Japanâs five-tier disaster warning system. It is used when people may already be facing life-threatening conditions and immediate action to secure safety is required.
Nagoya separately issued Level 5 emergency safety instructions in affected areas as the rain intensified.
The warnings were gradually lowered as river levels receded overnight, shifting the focus by Wednesday morning from immediate evacuation to damage assessment and relief.
Flooding hits Asian Games host city
The flooding also came at a sensitive time for Nagoya, which is preparing to co-host the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games from September 19. About 400 athletes and staff who had already arrived for the Games were temporarily moved to higher ground during the heavy rain. They later returned after the evacuation order was withdrawn.
More than 11,000 athletes from 45 countries and regions are expected to take part in the Games.
Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa said the Games venues had suffered no major damage, according to AP, although some facilities reported roof leaks. Organisers expect the event to proceed as scheduled.
With the highest flood alert lifted, authorities on Wednesday were turning to the scale of damage left by the September 8 downpour, even as relief measures under the Disaster Relief Act began to take effect.

title: Nearly 4,000 New York City students planted more than 100,000 beachgrass stalks across 2.25 acres at Coney Island Creek Park to rebuild protective dunes and help protect 50,000+ people from flooding
text:
Nearly 4,000 New York City public school students have taken part in an effort to restore protective dunes at Coney Island Creek Park in Brooklyn. Since 2022, students, teachers and community members have planted more than 100,000 American beachgrass culms across more than 2.25 acres of frontal dunes.
The project is part of the Resilient Schools and Communities (RiSC) programme run by the National Wildlife Federation (NWF). According to the organisation, it combines environmental education with habitat restoration and aims to help the local community prepare for flooding and other risks linked to extreme weather.
Coney Islandâs coastline has faced serious flooding during major storms. Superstorm Sandy in 2012 and Hurricane Ida in 2021 highlighted the risks faced by the area. The RiSC programme was launched in 2017 in seven South Brooklyn public schools, including schools in Coney Island, to help students understand these risks and learn about the environment around them.
The programme was also created to address gaps in climate education. At the time, students were receiving limited climate education, mainly through science classes, while resilience was not part of their curriculum. 
NWF developed a curriculum and a RiSC Vulnerability Assessment to help students understand how their schools and communities could be affected by climate-related risks and how those risks could be addressed.
How beachgrass can protect the coast
The restoration work focuses on American beachgrass, a native plant with a dense network of roots and rhizomes. These underground structures help the grass hold soil together. Its ability to stabilise dunes and reduce erosion has been documented, while the dunes can also provide coastal flood protection during extreme wave conditions.
The beachgrass also provides cover for wildlife found in Coney Island Creek Park, including snakes, small mammals and native and migratory birds.
Since 2022, habitat restoration events at the park have involved students, teachers, volunteers and community members. Nearly 4,000 public school students, more than 200 teachers and hundreds of community members have worked with NWF, NYC Parks, the American Littoral Society, corporate volunteers and Coney Islanders.
The planting effort has so far restored more than 2.25 acres of frontal dunes. Teachers are also brought to the site for professional development, connecting the restoration work with environmental education.
The programme aims to expand the plantings further, with the goal of building functional flood protection for more than 50,000 people living next to Coney Island Creek Park.
The organisation also wants the plantings to help stop sand from moving into roads, homes and sewer drains, as clogged drains can worsen flooding on streets.
Coney Island Creek Park
Lessons from Superstorm Sandy
The RiSC programme was shaped by what happened during Superstorm Sandy in October 2012. About 50,000 homes in Coney Island were left uninhabitable after the storm. Thousands of public housing residents were without heat and hot water for weeks, while an 11-foot storm surge brought polluted water and sand into homes and businesses.
The RiSC 3.0 curriculum was developed specifically for Coney Island. It was created with community leaders, teachers and scientific advisers and looked at the areaâs ecological and social history, as well as its vulnerability to coastal flooding.
The programme also draws on the role of dunes in protecting coastal communities. FEMA states that primary frontal dunes are often the first line of defence against flooding in coastal regions.
The plan is to continue planting native woody shrubs and trees in the maritime forest near the road. These plantings are expected to provide additional flood protection and sand stabilisation, while also creating more habitat for birds.
Coney Island Creek Park has also recorded a wide range of bird species. According to NWF, eBirders have documented 244 species in the park, including grebes, loons, gulls, terns, warblers, ducks and sandpipers.
Community support and long-term work
Community involvement has been central to the project. In November 2025, the organisation carried out extensive outreach in Coney Island before holding a meeting where residents could learn about the RiSC programme, ask questions and provide feedback.
The meeting was attended by students, community board members, representatives from four elected officialsâ offices and a homeowner association. NWF said feedback towards the programme was overwhelmingly positive, while continued shoreline restoration was identified as a top priority by the local community board.
The organisation has built relationships within the Coney Island community since 2020. NYC public schools have continued to support the habitat restoration work, while NYC Parks has helped with permits, staff, tools, plant material and other supplies.
Emily Fano, who leads the NYC project for NWF, said the organisation learned that working in a community with a history of disinvestment required patience and trust.
âI think about these four key things as a nonprofit coming into a frontline community like Coney Island that has experienced historic disinvestment: listen, be humble, earn trust, and ask what people need,â Fano said.
She said residents were involved in programme planning and design as paid advisers, while local educators and volunteers received stipends.
The organisation has committed to continuing its work in Coney Island until it is sure that the plantings provide functional flood protection.

title: When Nivin Pauly's house was submerged in 2018 floods; 'Bethlehem Kudumba Unit' star chose Nilambur teak for renovation
text:
Mollywood star 
Nivin Pauly
 is enjoying the success of Girish AD's 'Bethlehem Kudumba Unit'. The Malayalam film, which also stars Mamitha Baiju, has received rave responses from audiences and emerged as a superhit. With 'BKU', Nivin Pauly has made a massive comeback to Mollywood. Despite this success, the actor has faced several challenges on both personal and career fronts.
Nivin Pauly had previously spoken about the impact of the devastating 2018 Kerala floods on his family home. The actor revealed that his house in Aluva was submerged during the floods. He later renovated the property, choosing teak wood from Nilambur as part of the restoration.
Nivin Pauly recalls house being submerged in 2018 floods
The 2018 Kerala floods caused widespread destruction across the state. Nivin Pauly's family home in Aluva was also affected by the disaster. The actor had earlier recalled the difficulties caused by the flooding. His childhood home suffered damage and later required renovation.
Instead of simply restoring the property, Nivin Pauly incorporated a piece of Nilambur into his home. He opted to use traditional teak wood sourced from the region during the renovation.
Nivin Pauly chose Nilambur teak for his home
In January 2025, Nivin Pauly attended the 'Gokulam Night' event in Nilambur. He used the occasion to thank the people who had supported him during difficult periods.
According to a report by Hindustan Times, the actor spoke about the 2018 floods and their effect on his home. He also recalled the decision to use Nilambur teak while repairing the property. âThe trees from Nilambur are now part of my home,â he said. Nilambur is known for its teak plantations. For Nivin Pauly, the wood became a lasting part of his renovated family home.
Nivin Pauly explains absence from public events
During the same event, Nivin Pauly addressed his limited presence at public gatherings. He revealed that he had consciously stayed away from such appearances after facing personal challenges.
"The challenges I faced recently are well known. After those issues, I distanced myself from public events. However, when Gopalan Chettan, who has always been a mentor and guide to me, reached out, I didnât hesitate to come." Nivin Pauly also acknowledged the role played by Gopalan Chettan during difficult periods. His decision to attend the Nilambur event was linked to the relationship he shares with his mentor.
Nivin Pauly promises return with great films
The actor also used his appearance to express gratitude towards his supporters. He said their affection had remained important to him during challenging times.
âThis stage gives me the chance to express my heartfelt thanks to all of you. This year, I promise to come back with great films, and I trust that your support and love will remain unwavering."
Nivin Pauly's Aluva home and Kochi property
Nivin Pauly's family home in Aluva has a special place in his life. According to information shared by the Amma Kerala website, the property is his childhood home. It is also described as his permanent family residence. Reportedly, The actor also owns a luxury waterfront apartment in Thevara, Kochi.
Meanwhile, 'Bethlehem Kudumba Unit' has given Nivin Pauly another successful outing. The film has been receiving strong audience support since its release. Mamitha Baiju plays another main lead in the comedy entertainer.

title: Earthquake of magnitude 5.0 hits flood-ravaged Nepal
text:
NEW DELHI: An earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck Nepal at 9.38 pm on Tuesday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, as the region continues to grapple with the aftermath of devastating flash floods that have killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal.
The tremor was reported hours after a magnitude 5.3 earthquake struck Tibet, according to the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC). The Tibet quake occurred at a depth of 35 km.
The latest tremors come days after another earthquake of magnitude 5.0 struck Tibet on Thursday last week, according to data from the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ). That earthquake was recorded at a depth of 10 km.
The earthquakes come as the Tibet-Nepal region continues to reel from devastating flash floods that struck on August 26.
The floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border, sending a massive surge of water and debris downstream through the Bhotekoshi River. The disaster devastated settlements across northern and central Nepal and damaged several hydropower projects.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said the death toll from the floods had risen to 1,357 as of Tuesday, with rescue teams continuing searches for 5,326 people. 
A total of 13,583 people had been rescued.
Security forces recovered hundreds of bodies from affected districts including Chitawan, Nawalparasi East and West, Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Gorkha, Dhading and Tanahu. Authorities said 102 bodies had been handed over to families after identification and completion of legal formalities.
At least 43 people were also killed on the Chinese side, while more than 500 remained missing in Tibet, according to Chinese media reports.
The floods washed away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaged hydropower infrastructure. Rescue operations were also underway at hydropower projects where 121 people were believed to be trapped in underground tunnels.
The disaster has also raised concerns over the fragile environment of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, with Chinese climate experts pointing to rising temperatures, accelerated glacier melt, local geological and geomorphological conditions and broader climatic influences as possible contributing factors.
Sun Xiaoguang, head of the Meteorological Observatory of the Tibet Autonomous Region, said: âAccording to our monitoring, we can see the short-time rain days, or the imbalance of the rain pattern and the rising of the temperature in Tibet.â
He said the region could be affected by the climate change crisis and that extreme weather events in China could become more frequent.
Chinese officials said Tibet has about 33,000 glaciers, including 187 classified as high-risk and requiring round-the-clock satellite monitoring to predict possible collapses, according to PTI.
Kang Shichang, director and researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said glaciers across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau had shrunk by about 24% in area over the past six decades.
In the southern part of the plateau, including the Himalayas, glacier coverage had fallen by about 40% over the same period, Kang told Chinese daily The Paper, attributing the retreat primarily to global warming.
The scale of the disaster has also renewed scrutiny of hydropower projects in Tibet, including China's planned mega dam on the Brahmaputra River.
The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau is the source of around 10 transboundary rivers, including the Brahmaputra, making changes to its glaciers, rivers and extreme weather patterns significant for downstream regions.
Chinese researchers have linked the growing risks in the region to glacier retreat and climate change as authorities continue rescue and recovery operations following the August 26 floods.

title: Bihar floods worsen as over 34L affected across 13 districts
text:
PATNA: The flood situation in Bihar continued to deteriorate on Tuesday, with more than 34 lakh people affected across 13 districts. Authorities have issued an alert for downstream areas after the Ganga crossed the flood mark at Sultanganj in Bhagalpur district, according to news agency PTI.
A boat carrying 10 people capsized in the flood-hit Kharik Raghopur area of Bhagalpur on Tuesday morning. All those on board were rescued by personnel of the State Disaster Relief Force (SDRF), officials said.
According to the authorities, floods have so far affected around 34.31 lakh people in 480 gram panchayats spread across 13 districts. These include Patna, Bhagalpur, Vaishali, Saran, Begusarai, Khagaria and Munger.
The number of affected people was around 29.13 lakh on Monday, as overflowing rivers submerged large areas in the affected districts.
Bihar received 79.6 mm of rainfall in September so far, which is 31% above the normal level, according to the Bihar Meteorological Service Centre.
The Disaster Management Department said the Ganga at Sultanganj in Bhagalpur reached 36.80 metres at 8am on September 8, exceeding the previous Highest Flood Level (HFL) of 36.75 metres recorded on August 17, 2021. 
However, the department said the water level trend remained stable.
Several rivers in the state are currently flowing above danger levels at different locations. These include the Gandak, Kosi, Budhi Gandak, Ganga, Punpun, Bagmati and Ghaghra.
The Gandak is above the danger mark at Dumriaghat and Hajipur, while the Kosi has crossed the level at Baltara and Kursela. The Budhi Gandak is above the danger mark at Khagaria, while the Ganga has crossed it at Digha, Gandhi Ghat, Hathidah, Bhagalpur, Kahalgaon and Munger.
âA total of 432 community kitchens are currently being operated in various districts for flood-affected people. In addition, 14 relief camps are also being run, where arrangements have been made for accommodation, food, medical care and other essential services," the statement said.
The department said approximately 1.29 lakh polythene sheets and around 22,900 dry ration packets had been distributed to people affected by the floods.
Authorities are operating 1,832 boats for evacuation and transportation. Around 3,142 quintals of animal fodder have also been distributed, according to the Disaster Management Department.
The Gandak Barrage recorded a discharge of 1,04,400 cusecs at 10am on Tuesday, with the level remaining stable, the department said. The highest discharge recorded at the barrage this year was 2,24,000 cusecs on July 14.
At the Kosi Barrage, the discharge was 1,69,985 cusecs at 10am, with the trend showing a decline. Its highest discharge so far this year was 2,55,425 cusecs, recorded on July 20.
For rescue and relief operations, 27 SDRF teams and 10 NDRF teams have been deployed across various districts.

title: Tejashwi urges PM to declare Bihar floods national disaster, seeks Rs 5kcr package
text:
Patna:
 Leader of opposition Tejashwi Prasad Yadav on Monday urged Prime Minister 
Narendra Modi
 to declare Biharâs flood situation a ânational disasterâ and provide a Rs 5,000-crore central assistance package for relief, rescue and rehabilitation operations.
In a letter to the PM after visiting flood-hit diara areas, Tejashwi said rising river levels and widespread inundation had affected millions of people, disrupting normal life and damaging public infrastructure.
He alleged that the state govtâs relief and rescue efforts were inadequate compared with the scale of the crisis and accused NDA leaders in the state of failing to press the Centre for additional assistance.

Seeking long-term measures, he proposed a Flood Resilience Mission for Bihar focusing on river and embankment management, drainage improvement, revival of water bodies and modern flood forecasting systems. He also stressed the need for stronger water-management coordination with Nepal and other neighbouring countries.
The opposition leader further sought an independent review of Biharâs disaster-management preparedness and utilisation of contingency funds. title: India’s esports & gaming community rallies as S8UL’s Gulrez Khan raises Rs 4.85 lakh for Nepal relief and supports flood-hit Assam
text:
S8UL Esports gamer Gulrez Khan, popularly known as Joker Ki Haveli, brought together the gaming and esports community to support flood relief efforts. While digital platforms have enabled creators to mobilise large communities around causes within hours, Joker Ki Haveliâs continued involvement on the ground highlights how that collective support can translate into tangible assistance for affected families.
For a gamer whose work is rooted in building and engaging a digital community, these efforts represent another dimension of that relationship. The response to the Nepal charity stream demonstrated the ability of the gaming and esports community to come together around a cause, while the ongoing work in Assam has taken that support from the digital space into affected communities themselves.

title: Pandu river floods Kanpur; 40,000 affected, homes submerged under up to 6 feet of water
text:
KANPUR: Flooding caused by the swelling Pandu river has brought life to a standstill in parts of Kanpur and neighbouring Kanpur Dehat, with nearly 40,000 people and more than 1,000 houses affected.
Streets in some areas are submerged under 5-7 feet of water, while water has entered houses up to six feet.
Several families have evacuated, while some residents remain stranded on rooftops or have taken shelter under plastic sheets, news agency PTI reported.
At the Kanpur Barrage, the upstream water level was recorded at 114.200 metres, crossing the warning mark of 114 metres and nearing the danger level of 115 metres, Kanpur District Magistrate Jitendra Pratap Singh told PTI.
The downstream level stood at 113.930 metres, while the discharge was recorded at 3,59,202 cusecs, against the danger-level discharge of 5,44,373 cusecs, he said.
Families evacuated as homes, huts submerged
Floodwaters have entered several residential areas. In Varun Vihar, low-lying houses have been inundated and some huts damaged.
Water has entered tin-roofed structures up to five feet, forcing displaced families to set up shelters using plastic sheets along the Gujaini canal with only essential belongings, PTI reported.
During an inspection, senior officials saw children eating whatever food was available and women washing utensils near water tankers.
Livestock was also being kept alongside families in the makeshift shelters.
The administration has set up a relief camp in Barra-8 for residents of Mayapuram, Ravidaspuram and Varun Vihar. The district magistrate and local MLA Surendra Maithani distributed relief material among affected families.
NDRF rescues hundreds in Pipauri
In Pipauri village, more than 200 houses have been affected.
The NDRF launched rescue operations after the river rose rapidly on Thursday night and evacuated hundreds of residents. Water has entered some houses up to six feet, with rescue operations continuing, PTI reported.
The district magistrate inspected Pipauri three days ago, while sub-divisional magistrate (Sadar) Anubhav Singh surveyed the inundated areas by motorboat for about an hour.
In Bihari Purwa in Bidhnu block, a school has been submerged under nearly six feet of water, while several lanes are under 8-10 feet of water.
Some residents have moved to safer locations, while those unable to leave have taken shelter on rooftops covered with plastic sheets.
Floodwaters cut off Bikru-Shivli route
The flooding has also cut off the Bikru-Shivli route after a makeshift bridge was submerged.
The Pandu is flowing 2-3 feet above the bridge, forcing residents of Bikru, Takipur Devkali, Kanjati, Kanshiram Purwa, Bachipur and Sakhrej to take a longer route to reach Shivli market.
Several villages in the Shivli area, including Majhihar, Mogra, Ramgarh, Singhpur Shivli, Bakaspurwa, Hardiya Nala, Kailai and Mawaiya, have also reported waterlogging.
Agriculture has also been affected.
Around 250 bighas of paddy and millet crops have been submerged in Bhagga Niwada, residents Sonu Singh, Govardhan Singh and Jaichand Singh said.
Water has also entered low-lying areas and agricultural fields in Kheda Kursi village in Rasulabad.
Temples surrounded by floodwaters
In Gangadin Niwada, the Ram Dham temple is surrounded by water, forcing devotees to wade through dirty water to offer prayers, villagers Bhola Awasthi and Dipendra Mishra said.
Similarly, the Ganesh temple at Kursi Kheda near Torna market has been engulfed by floodwaters.
Residents are concerned about difficulties during Ganesh Mahotsav and other upcoming religious events if the water does not recede soon, villager Monti Dixit said.
In Rasulabad, sub-divisional magistrate Abhishek Kumar and Tehsildar Pankaj Upadhyay, along with revenue officials, visited villages along the river on Saturday and assessed the situation.
Villagers were informed about a relief centre at the primary school in Paliya-Bans Kheda, where people can be shifted if the situation worsens, Kumar said.
Health teams step up disease-control measures
The administration has also intensified health and sanitation measures in flood-affected areas.
The district magistrate directed officials to maintain special surveillance, organise health camps and carry out fogging and vector-control measures.
During an inspection of the flood-hit Mardanpur village in Bidhnu block, Community Health Centre superintendent Neeraj Sachan said daily health camps were being organised and source-reduction activities undertaken.
Health teams are examining residents, including those with fever, and providing medicines as required.
In urban areas, evening fogging is being conducted, while bleaching powder is being spread in rural areas. Indoor space spraying and larvicidal treatment of drains are also being carried out.
The administration has also ordered entomological surveys, larval-control measures and awareness campaigns in the affected areas, officials said.

title: Gautam Buddha’s warning echoes as Ganga floods city
text:
Patna: More than two millennia ago, when Pataligama, modern Patna, was little more than a settlement on the banks of the Ganga, 
Gautama Buddha
 is said to have foreseen its transformation into a great city and warned that it would remain vulnerable to fire, floods and internal discord.
Today, as the Ganga swells around Patna and large parts of 
Bihar
 again face the threat of inundation, that ancient warning sounds less like a distant prophecy and more like an uncomfortable reminder from history.
More than five million people in 14 districts of north Bihar have already been affected by floods this year, with breaches in embankments worsening the situation. Patna, too, is increasingly vulnerable as the Ganga rises and low-lying areas come under pressure.
For Bihar, floods are nothing new. Nearly 68,800 sq km, more than 70% of the stateâs geographical area, is considered flood-prone, making Bihar Indiaâs most flood-affected state. The rivers that have enriched its fertile plains with fresh alluvial deposits have also repeatedly brought devastation.
The irony is that decades of attempts to âcontrolâ these rivers through embankments have done little to eliminate the problem.
When the National Flood Control Policy was introduced in 1954, Bihar had about 160 km of embankments and around 2.5 million hectares were considered flood-prone. By 2004, the embankment network had expanded to about 3,465 km, but the flood-prone area had risen to nearly 6.89 million hectares.
Patna University geology expert Atul Aditya Pandey described the impact of embankments as disastrous, arguing that riverbeds in several north Bihar rivers have risen because natural river processes have been obstructed. Even areas supposedly protected from floods suffer from waterlogging and salinity.
Former Geological Survey of India director N Dayal said Biharâs flood problem cannot be addressed without understanding the regionâs extraordinary geological setting â the worldâs youngest and steepest mountain system, the Himalayas, followed by an exceptionally flat alluvial plain.
âAny flood management system should essentially take note of this feature,â he stressed.
Retired NIT Patna civil engineering teacher Santosh Kumar argued technology should be used not merely to obstruct floods but to harness their benefits through better land-use planning. âA riverâs natural regime should be given its due appreciation before embarking on any engineering response to contain it,â he said.
He also advocated rejuvenating Biharâs traditional âdharsâ â natural channels that once carried floodwater and provided drainage.
The Kosi offers the most dramatic warning. Known as the âSorrow of Biharâ, it breached its embankment at Kusaha in Nepal in 2008 and reclaimed an old channel, affecting millions.
The message from history is stark: Bihar cannot permanently imprison its rivers, Kumar said.

title: The annual Delhi Yamuna flood threat- why September matters?
text:
2025: People, animals living near floodplains relocated on roads ( on left); Yamuna Flood plain board (on right) (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)
A year after the Yamuna inundated large parts of Delhi, the river is again flowing above the danger mark. The immediate threat may be lower this time, but heavy rain in the upper catchment could quickly change the picture, exposing how vulnerable the cityâs floodplain still remains.That vulnerability is built into Delhiâs geography. Every monsoon, as September sets in, the city watches the Yamuna closely because even a sharp rise in the river or a sudden surge in upstream discharge can quickly put thousands living and working along the floodplains at risk.The danger mark at the Old Iron Railway Bridge is 205.33 metres, while evacuation of vulnerable residents begins when the river reaches around 206 metres. On September 6, the Yamuna was flowing at 205.59 metres, already slightly above the danger mark.And it is not just the people living along the river who feel the impact. When the Yamuna rises sharply, critical roads and infrastructure can also be affected. The Loha Pul, a vital link between Central Delhi (including Kashmere Gate and Old Delhi Railway Station) and East Delhi, is among the key crossings vulnerable to rising waters during severe floods.
2025: When the Yamuna broke its banks
Last year, the warning turned into a full-blown crisis.The Yamuna crossed the danger mark and rose above 207 metres, inundating several low-lying parts of the Capital and forcing more than 10,000 people to evacuate vulnerable areas.
The warning numbers you should know
The impact extended well beyond flooded homes. Roads and public infrastructure were affected, electricity supplies were disrupted and houses were left covered in mud and silt after the water receded. Thousands whose livelihoods depended on the floodplain also took a hit.Floodwaters reached the Ring Road and Outer Ring Road, disrupting traffic between Majnu ka Tilla and the Salimgarh bypass. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi stopped cremations at Nigambodh Ghat and the Geeta Colony ground because of flooding. Water-treatment infrastructure was also affected.A major factor was the enormous volume of water released from the Hathnikund Barrage in Haryana after intense rainfall in the upper Yamuna catchment.
2026: Is Delhi facing another repeat?
A year later, attention is once again turning to the Yamuna.The monsoon remains active, with heavy rain reported in parts of Delhi and northern India. The immediate concern is not simply the riverâs current level, but how much water is being released upstream and whether intense rainfall in the catchment pushes those levels sharply higher.The Yamuna has remained comparatively stable this year, despite crossing the danger mark.
2025 vs 2026 of Yamuna flood threat
Dr Shiv Singh Rawat, water expert and convener of the WalkForYamuna Campaign, said the difference becomes clearer when the upstream discharge is examined. âThis yearâs situation needs to be understood in its proper hydrological context. The maximum discharge released from Hathnikund Barrage during this year was around 64,000 cusecs, which is significantly below an extreme flood situation. That helps explain why Delhi experienced a much less severe river-flood situation than in 2025.âBut that relative stability offers no guarantee.The India Meteorological Department has warned of isolated heavy rainfall over Haryana, Chandigarh and Delhi from September 10-12.Fairly widespread rain, accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning, is also likely over Uttarakhand from September 6-12, while rainfall disturbances are expected over Himachal Pradesh.For Delhi, what happens upstream can matter as much as what happens within the Capital itself.A spell of intense rainfall in the upper catchment can send a surge downstream, leaving communities along the floodplain with limited time to respond.
The flood threat does not end with the water level
The relatively stable Yamuna this year may have given Delhi a temporary reprieve, but the underlying vulnerability remains.The floodplain is not simply vacant land beside the river.It acts as a natural buffer during floods, helps recharge groundwater and performs an important ecological function.
Know how a Yamuna flood unfolds in Delhi
âThe 2-km-stretch on both sides of Yamuna acts as a buffer for floods, restores groundwater balance and acts as an organic filter. However, excess rain will create flooding in Delhi, and sanitation is not adequate to handle floods in the Capital,â says environmentalist Kavita Ashok.Rawat warns that the greater danger could emerge gradually through construction and development. âThe concern is that areas outside the most restrictive floodplain zones could gradually become corridors for permanent construction, infrastructure and commercial riverfront activity,â he says. âThat would undermine the very floodplain functions that protect the city.âThe question, therefore, is not only whether the Yamuna will rise this September. It is whether Delhi is becoming more or less vulnerable when it does.
Living with the Yamuna
For families living along Delhiâs floodplain, the monsoon is not simply a season of heavy rain. It is a recurring threat of displacement.When the river rises, families may have to move their belongings, livestock and essentials to higher ground with little warning.
The granddaughter of Ramu Sahni, who lives with his family near the Yamuna floodplain, told TOI that residents donât receive any advance warning.âWe receive no warning on time. We see the rise in the water level of Yamuna and ourselves decide to shift to the roads with all our belongings. The authorities then notice the crowd on the roads and help us with tents.âSahni, who came to Delhi from Bihar in search of employment many years ago, says the relief arrangements have also changed. âEarlier, they used to provide us with some ration and water in tents but now the situation has changed,â he says. âI donât live here for free, I pay rent.â
Houses built around Delhi Yamuna Floodplain (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)
For many residents, simply relocating permanently is not an easy option.Their lives are tied to the floodplain through work, transport, markets and social networks. When the water recedes, they return.âWe return back here when the water recedes after 2 months. This is all we have. I run a rickshaw, we are mostly ragpickers. Where will we go?âThat cycle of evacuation, waiting, returning and rebuilding has become part of life for many families.
Animals: The overlooked victims
For families with livestock, evacuation is even more complicated.Leaving home is one thing. Moving buffaloes, cattle, calves and other animals to safety is another. Stray animals are even more vulnerable, particularly when rising water cuts off their escape routes.
Buffaloes in the river | Fencing installed (Pic credit: Priyanka Jaiswal)
Sahni says livestock is not simply property for floodplain families, it is their livelihood. âPeople usually take their buffaloes with them on the roads. How will they earn? Now they have installed fencing around a small Yamuna pond here. How will buffaloes go there? They need to be there for survival. If a flood comes right now, there is no way we can rescue them immediately as there is only a small route to travel.âWhen asked who rescues stray animals during floods, he had no clear answer.PETA India told TOI that animals stranded during floods can face exhaustion, dehydration, hunger, injury and drowning, making rapid rescue and access to food, clean water and veterinary care critical.âThe biggest challenge when trying to reach animals in emergency situations is getting to them in the first place. Access may be cut off by rising water, for instance,â said Sachin Bangera of PETA India.During last yearâs floods, PETA Indiaâs Rapid Response Team arranged a boat to rescue dogs stranded in flooded areas and at risk of drowning.âAnimals who are left chained are the most vulnerable because they cannot escape, or they become exhausted and drown,â Bangera said.
Aditi Bakshi, Animal Welfare Advocate and Specialist - Government and Public Policy at Mercy For Animals, says the problem goes deeper than rescue.âMany people are forced into an impossible choice by a system that gives them no option. Rescue boats and relief camps do not take animals. When the administration tells a family to evacuate and will not let them bring their cow, their pigs, or their two goats, the family has to choose between their childrenâs safety and the animalâs life.âShe argues that flood preparedness must explicitly include animals.According to Bakshi, Delhi lacks a comprehensive operational framework covering animal evacuation, including a nodal officer, mapped animal shelters, pre-monsoon fodder stocks, evacuation protocols for large animals and regular drills. âA plan that has never been drilled is not a plan; it is a document,â she says.
Delhiâs real test: Preparing before the next flood
For Delhiâs floodplain residents, the Yamuna may rise for only a few days. The disruption can last months.That makes flood preparedness about far more than issuing warnings once the river begins to rise.âRelief must be immediate, but rehabilitation must be humane and sustainable. People should not have to repeatedly rebuild their lives every monsoon,â says Dr Heera Lal Patel, IAS.During a flood emergency, he says, authorities need to provide clear information, accessible evacuation routes, transport and safe shelters. Vulnerable families cannot be expected to organise an evacuation on their own.Rawat argues that Delhi needs scientifically determined, risk-based floodplain zoning.âThe real measures of success are: how many people are taken out of high-risk locations, flood-storage capacity restored and new encroachment prevented.â
For companion-animal guardians, PETA India recommends identifying safe locations where pets will be accepted, keeping an emergency kit ready, and ensuring animals are microchipped or wear collars with updated contact details.But the larger challenge is institutional.The Yamunaâs rise is predictable. The exact scale and timing of a flood may not be.For communities living beside the river, that distinction can mean the difference between having time to evacuate and scrambling for safety as the water arrives.And every September, Delhi faces the same question: when the Yamuna rises again, will the city be better prepared, or will thousands once again be forced to leave their lives behind?

title: 19 lakh lives impacted as Ganga breaches flood mark in Patna
text:
The Ganga was flowing at 50.57 metres at Gandhi Ghat at 6am on Sunday, 0.05 metres above its previous highest flood level (HFL) of 50.52 metres recorded on August 21, 2016.
NEW DELHI: More than 19.57 lakh people have been affected by floods across 11 districts of Bihar as of Sunday, with authorities putting downstream areas on high alert. This comes after the Ganga, following heavy rain, crossed its previous highest flood level at Gandhi Ghat in Patna.The Ganga was flowing at 50.57 metres at Gandhi Ghat at 6am on Sunday, 0.05 metres above its previous highest flood level (HFL) of 50.52 metres recorded on August 21, 2016. While the trend was stable at Gandhi Ghat, authorities warned that Hathidah and subsequent gauge stations could be affected over the next one to three days.
The rising water levels have prompted heightened vigilance across several downstream districts, with officials monitoring river levels, embankments, vulnerable locations and low-lying areas and keeping rescue machinery ready.
19.57 lakh people affected across 11 districts
According to officials, flooding has affected around 19.57 lakh people in 330 gram panchayats across Patna, Bhojpur, Saran, Vaishali, Bhagalpur, Begusarai, Buxar, Samastipur, Munger, Katihar and Araria.The latest figures indicate a worsening impact compared with earlier assessments, when around 16.85 lakh people across 61 blocks and 300 gram panchayats had been reported affected.With several rivers continuing to flow above danger levels, authorities have intensified relief and rescue operations in the affected districts.
The Water Resources Department has warned that the Ganga at Hathidah may also cross its previous HFL, increasing the risk for Begusarai, Lakhisarai, Munger, Bhagalpur and Katihar.âOfficials and field-level authorities have been directed to remain alert and continuously monitor water levels, embankments, vulnerable locations and low-lying areas, while taking precautionary measures as required.âEngineers have been asked to keep flood-control resources and machinery ready. People in affected areas have been advised to avoid going near the river and remain cautious,â the advisory stated.Local administrations have also been asked to keep a close watch on boat operations, prevent overloading and ensure residents receive regular updates about the flood situation.
Ganga breaches danger levels at several locations
The Ganga is above the danger mark at several locations in Bihar.At Buxar, the river was 0.08 metres above the danger mark, although its level was declining. At Dighaghat in Patna, it was 1.54 metres above the danger mark, while at Gandhi Ghat it stood 1.96 metres above it.At Hathidah, the Ganga was 1.74 metres above the danger mark and continued to rise. Munger recorded a level 0.51 metres above the danger mark, with the river showing a rising trend.The river was also 2.01 metres above the danger mark at Sultanganj and 0.65 metres above it at Bhagalpur. The Ganga remained above the danger mark at Kahalgaon as well.At Pandarak in Patna, the river was flowing at 43.92 metres at 6 am, 0.19 metres above its previous HFL of 43.73 metres recorded on August 16, 2021.In contrast, the Ganga remained below the warning level in Prayagraj and Varanasi. Its level was rising in Prayagraj but declining in Varanasi.
Several rivers remain above danger levels
The flood threat is not confined to the Ganga. Several other rivers in Bihar are also flowing above their respective danger levels.The Gandak is above the danger mark at Dumariaghat and Hajipur, while the Kosi has crossed the mark at Baltara and Kursela. The Budhi Gandak is above the danger level at Khagaria.The Punpun is above the danger mark at Sripalpur, while the Bagmati has crossed it at Benibad. The Ghaghra is also flowing above the danger level at Darauli.The combination of rising river levels and further rainfall has kept authorities on alert, particularly in downstream and low-lying areas.
Relief operations expanded across flood-hit districts
The administration has deployed significant resources to assist people affected by the floods.A total of 110 community kitchens are currently operating in various districts to provide food to affected residents. Earlier official figures had put the number of operational community kitchens at 80, with around 1.21 lakh people receiving meals through them.One relief camp is also operational, providing accommodation, food, medical assistance and other essential facilities to 326 flood-affected people.Authorities have distributed around 45,900 polythene sheets and 11,700 dry ration packets as part of relief efforts.Boats are being used extensively to evacuate residents and maintain movement in areas affected by rising waters. The latest deployment stands at 1,345 boats across the state, compared with 1,158 reported earlier.
SDRF, NDRF teams deployed
With the possibility of further flooding, 27 State Disaster Response Force teams and 10 National Disaster Response Force teams have been deployed across different districts.The teams have been tasked with undertaking rapid relief and rescue operations, while district administrations continue to monitor vulnerable areas and river embankments.Officials have also been instructed to ensure that flood-control equipment and machinery remain ready for deployment as required.
Rain forecast raises concern over further rise
The flood situation could remain challenging over the coming days as the Bihar Meteorological Service Centre has forecast light to moderate rainfall at several places across the state over the next two days.Heavy rainfall is also possible at some locations.Authorities are therefore preparing for the possibility of further increases in river levels, particularly in areas already affected by flooding. The state government and district administrations are continuing to monitor the situation and deploy relief materials, boats and rescue teams according to local requirements.
Rail services affected on Patna-Gaya section
The flooding has also disrupted railway operations in parts of the state.The East Central Railway said on Sunday that some trains had been cancelled or diverted because of the âalarmingly high water level at bridge number 21" connecting Punpun and Parsa Bazar stations on the Patna-Gaya section.The development adds to the disruption caused by rising waters as authorities continue to focus on evacuation, relief and the safety of residents in flood-affected areas.
Barrage discharge data recorded at 9 am on Sunday showed that the Sone Barrage at Indrapuri was releasing 2,27,739 cusecs of water, although the flow was declining.The Kosi Barrage at Birpur was releasing 1,68,400 cusecs, with the discharge remaining stable. The Gandak Barrage at Valmikinagar was releasing 1,29,000 cusecs, also with a stable trend.With multiple rivers remaining above danger levels, further rainfall forecast over the next two days and the Ganga already having crossed its previous HFL at Gandhi Ghat, authorities have urged residents in vulnerable areas to remain cautious and avoid approaching swollen rivers.

title: China silences flood victims to spotlight Xi Jinping's rescue efforts
text:
More than a week after a deadly flash flood tore through valleys along the China-Nepal border, the scale of the disaster is becoming clearer, but on the Chinese side, the victims themselves remain largely unseen. Reports indicate that China is exerting extreme pressure to monitor reporting surrounding the disaster.
The disaster has killed more than 1,300 people and left more than 5,600 missing across the two countries, according to the latest figures cited in reports. Yet China has released information about the disaster slowly and tightly controlled access to affected areas, offering little public detail about those who died or remain missing.
Chinese authorities' death toll update on Friday, raised the number killed in Tibet to 31 and said 531 people remained unaccounted for. An earlier update had put the toll at 21 dead and 541 missing, including 261 foreigners from 23 countries.
The information vacuum has drawn attention to China's longstanding restrictions on reporting natural disasters, restrictions that are particularly severe in Tibet, where communications are closely monitored and foreign journalists require special permission to travel.
Chinese state media outlets Xinhua and CCTV have been allowed into the affected areas, but their coverage has largely focused on the government's rescue and relief response. Reports have highlighted President Xi Jinping's instructions, rescuers working in difficult conditions and the logistics of delivering aid, rather than identifying victims or giving families a public platform.
Human Rights Watch said some Chinese journalists had been instructed not to interview relatives of people killed or missing and to rely only on material provided by Xinhua.
The Associated Press said it requested permission to visit the affected areas soon after the disaster but had not been granted access.
The restrictions have also extended to social media. Chinese state media circulated details of 10 cases in which people across the country were detained or fined for allegedly spreading rumours about the disaster. Punishments included police detention of between five and 10 days, with some people also fined.
One social media post questioned the official death toll, claiming that far more people had been swept away than authorities had reported.
Stark contrast to Nepalese coverage
The response stands in stark contrast to neighbouring Nepal, where authorities have provided regular updates on those killed, missing and rescued. The Nepalese army has released footage of helicopter rescues and survivors being pulled from mud-filled hydropower tunnels, while journalists have been able to visit affected sites, rescue camps and burial grounds.
The difference was underscored by the rescue of a Chinese national from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal on Saturday, 10 days after the disaster. The man, identified by the army only as Luhaitao, was found alive inside a 225-metre tunnel at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project.
Video released by the Nepali army showed rescuers giving him medical attention inside a helicopter before taking him to an army hospital. He appeared exhausted and disoriented, with mud and dust covering his clothes and skin.
On the Nepalese side, families have also been able to make their own searches public, with some holding symbolic burial rites for relatives whose bodies have not been recovered.
On the Chinese side, however, relatives of missing people have had far fewer avenues to seek information publicly. An independent Chinese media outlet operating in exile interviewed families of missing Chinese nationals, including Peng Guangming, a young man working on a Chinese-supported highway project in Nepal. Peng was last in contact with a colleague about 10 minutes before the flood.
Another missing Chinese national, He Hongrong, was last seen on the Nepal side carrying a green backpack and waiting to cross into China. Her family has circulated her photograph online in the hope that someone can provide information about her whereabouts.
The tight control is especially significant in Tibet, a Chinese autonomous region that has experienced decades of political unrest and government repression. Foreign travel there requires special permission, while restrictions on communications make it difficult for Tibetans to freely share information with people outside China.
China has also previously faced criticism for slow-moving disaster reporting. After severe flooding in Guangxi in July, authorities increased the official death toll more than a month later from 39 to 159.
The difference in reporting exposes how China lets victims become invisible in order to protect the state machinery.

title: UP boy donates piggy bank savings for Nepal flood victims

title: Three women were caught in a deadly Grand Canyon flash flood and clung to a rock ledge for 5 hours; after briefly believing each other had been swept away, a helicopter found them alive
text:
A routine hike through the Grand Canyon turned into a fight for survival when a sudden flash flood sent torrents of muddy water, rocks and debris through the canyon. Three women found themselves trapped during the storm and spent about five hours clinging to a rock ledge, uncertain whether they would make it out alive. At one point, they were separated from one another and each feared the others had been swept away by the floodwaters. According to 98 Rock Online, the survivors were sisters Jessica Buscher and Melanie McGuirk and their friend Katie Brink. The flood struck at about 2:30 p.m. Saturday, forcing them to take shelter on a ledge and hold on as water and debris moved through the canyon. Their ordeal eventually ended when a rescue helicopter spotted them and brought them to safety.
The storm arrived quickly
The three women had begun their hike expecting an ordinary day in one of America's most famous landscapes. Instead, conditions changed dramatically when the monsoon storm intensified. Heavy rain began pouring through the canyon, turning normally passable areas into dangerous channels for fast-moving water. The women sheltered beneath a rock formation as the flood swept through the area.
According to 98 Rock Online, the women later recounted their experience, including the moment they lost sight of one another and feared they had been swept away. 
Brink described the experience as holding on "just with my fingertips" while being repeatedly splashed with mud. McGuirk recalled hearing boulders tumbling through the canyon, with the ground shaking beneath them. The danger was not limited to the water itself. Floodwaters carried mud, rocks, branches and other debris, creating additional hazards for anyone caught below.
They thought one was gone
The most frightening part of the ordeal came when the three friends became separated. Buscher and McGuirk lost sight of Brink and believed their friend had been carried away. Brink, meanwhile, thought the same thing had happened to the sisters.
For roughly 20 minutes, Brink believed she was alone. The sisters eventually saw Brink again when she came around a bend in the trail. The reunion brought an unexpected moment of relief after each had feared they had lost the others. But the danger was far from over. The women remained stranded for hours as they waited for a way out of the canyon. Rescue helicopters were already operating in the area, searching for hikers who had been trapped by the flooding.
Helicopter finally spots them
After about five hours of clinging to the ledge and waiting for help, the women were finally spotted by a rescue helicopter. According to their account, a helicopter initially looked toward them before returning roughly 45 minutes later. The crew then reached the women and transported them to safety.
Their rescue was part of a much larger emergency response unfolding across the Grand Canyon. The Arizona Department of Public Safety said its Ranger 3 helicopter completed 13 flights to the canyon floor and back to the South Rim Helibase, transporting 61 hikers to safety.
A deadly Grand Canyon flood
The women's survival came amid a much broader disaster. A severe flash flood struck the Grand Canyon on August 29 after intense rainfall, sending water and debris through the Bright Angel Creek area. The flooding destroyed or damaged trails and footbridges and left hikers scrambling for higher ground.
The disaster also proved fatal. Two people died, while at least one other person remained unaccounted for during the early stages of the search. More than 80 people were eventually airlifted from the canyon, according to the Associated Press (AP). The scale of the flooding was especially dangerous because conditions could change within minutes. Hikers interviewed by AP described strong winds, torrential rain, hail, falling rocks and rapidly moving water. Some said the storm appeared to intensify with little warning.
Damage beyond the hikers
The flooding did not only threaten people in the canyon. It also caused extensive damage to infrastructure. Footbridges were washed away, trails were damaged and large amounts of mud and debris were carried through the canyon. One of the most serious consequences was damage to the Transcanyon Waterline, the major pipeline supplying water to areas of the park.
The destruction forced officials to begin assessing the damage while rescue and recovery operations continued. For Buscher, McGuirk and Brink, however, the immediate concern was simply getting through the storm alive. Their story stands out among dozens of dramatic rescues because of the brief but terrifying moment when each woman believed she had lost the other two. After hours of holding on and waiting, the appearance of the helicopter turned a desperate situation into a rescue. They survived a flood that killed others nearby, leaving them deeply aware of how quickly conditions in the canyon can become life-threatening.
