title: Nepal estimates $2.56 billion flood damage, faces $52.6 million recovery cost
text:
Nepal has estimated that the devastating floods that hit the country last week caused at least $2.56 billion in damage to property, housing and infrastructure. The government also expects to spend another $52.6 million on early recovery, officials said on Friday.
The damage estimate, equivalent to 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees, covers homes, roads and other critical infrastructure destroyed or damaged in the floods. The initial recovery cost of 7.95 billion rupees will cover work over the first four months, including rebuilding roads, setting up temporary shelters and restoring drinking water and electricity.
The scale of the destruction has left thousands displaced and added pressure on rescue and relief operations.
Thousands remain displaced
More than 4,500 people displaced by the floods are currently living in 38 relief centres across Nepal.
For many survivors, however, basic needs remain difficult to meet. People in some camps have struggled to obtain essential medicines and cash, even as authorities distribute food and other relief supplies.
Suresh Kumar Karanjit, who is staying at a relief centre in Devighat in badly affected Nuwakot district, lost his younger brother in the floods. 
He said the centre did not have the medicine prescribed for his heart condition.
Karanjit eventually raised money for his regular medicine by selling a carton of noodles he had received as relief for 400 rupees, or about $2.60.
âWe have been living here for a week. The relief materials are being provided, which is good. But there is a lack of medicine,â he said.
Nepal's disaster authority chief Dharma Raj Uprety said health centres staffed by doctors and stocked with medicines had been established at each shelter. Authorities were also prioritising hygiene and sanitation to limit the spread of disease.
Roads and bridges destroyed
The Aug. 26 floods devastated towns and valleys across Nepal, destroying homes, roads, bridges and other vital infrastructure.
The floods were likely triggered by a glacier collapse, according to authorities.
At least 1,259 people have been killed and more than 5,000 remain missing, Nepal's disaster management agency said. On the Tibet side of the border, China said 21 people had been killed and 541 remained missing as of late Wednesday.
The destruction has also cut off several communities from normal transport routes.
In Bidur, a town along the Trishuli River, residents have been using a temporary zip line to cross the river. Army personnel have been helping people use the makeshift crossing and assisting them on the opposite bank.
Rescue teams search hydroelectric tunnels
In a long-awaited breakthrough, two workers were also rescued from the Trishula 3A hydropower tunnel. Nepal's energy minister shared the updates on the workers trapped for nine days. Workers have begun manually opening the upper section of the passage, according to lawmaker Ram Neupane.
An access road was constructed over the past week to reach the excavation site. But rescuers still face major obstacles. More rock blasting and debris removal will be required before heavy machinery can be brought to the area.
Rescue operations have also shifted towards several hydroelectric projects where workers are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.
About 900 workers remain missing. Specialised rescue teams from India, China and the United States are taking part in efforts to reach them.
Recovery effort begins
The government's early recovery estimate highlights the immediate financial burden created by the disaster.
Upreti said the projected $52.6 million would be needed during the first four months to restore essential services and provide temporary support to affected communities.
The longer-term cost is expected to be far higher, given the scale of damage to housing, roads and infrastructure and the continuing search for missing people.

title: When Dm asked the entire locality to vacate amid flood fears, this is what this Chitrakoot priest did
text:
Chitrakoot: The water was rising, the river was in spate and officials were urging people to move to safety. But inside the flooded premises of a temple at Ramghat, a priest chose to stay back.
As the swollen 
Mandakini
 River submerged parts of Chitrakoot, District Magistrate Pulkit Garg and Superintendent of Police Arun Kumar Singh reached the Bada Math temple on Tuesday and appealed to the priest to leave the premises. The two senior officials reportedly folded their hands and urged him to move to a safer place.
The priest, however, refused. His answer was that he could not leave the deity behind. The emotional exchange took place as the Mandakini continued to rise after around 36 hours of heavy rain in the hilly areas. The river was flowing around five metres above the danger mark, with floodwater entering several temples, monasteries, shops and homes around the famous Ramghat area.
âI have spent my whole life at Godâs feetâ
According to reports, the officials tried to persuade the priest to leave along with other members of the temple. Some people eventually moved out, but the priest remained inside.
He told the officials that his entire life had been spent in the service of God and questioned how he could abandon the deity at a time when the temple itself was surrounded by floodwater. 
He told the officials that whatever happened would happen according to God's will.
The response left the officials with little choice. After spending considerable time trying to convince him, the administrative team returned to continue its larger rescue operation in the flood-hit area.
The episode was captured on video and subsequently circulated widely on social media, bringing attention to the unusual scene from flood-hit Chitrakoot.
With the Mandakini overflowing, authorities stepped up rescue and evacuation efforts in Ramghat and neighbouring areas. Teams were using boats to bring people stranded inside their homes to safer locations, while announcements through loudspeakers urged residents in vulnerable areas to move out. The National Disaster Response Force and other rescue teams were also kept active as the administration monitored the situation.
As per reports, the river level later showed some decline, but continuing rain meant the danger had not completely passed.

title: ‘Come to Nepal, brother’: Sonu Sood replies to journalist's 'marketing' jibe over flood relief work
text:
Nepal has been reeling from devastating floods that have claimed numerous lives, leaving families grieving while several others remain unaccounted for. Amid the widespread struggle to recover, actor 
Sonu Sood
 made his way to Nepal to show solidarity with those affected and lend a hand in relief work. He also posted photos from the trip, looking at his efforts to support flood victims.
Sonu Sood faces backlash over visit
Sonuâs visit to Nepal drew mixed reactions, with praise pouring in from some quarters while others responded with skepticism. Among the critics was journalist Ajit Anjum, who took to social media to share his views. "If this isn't Sonu Sood's marketing, if not, then what is it? Just arrived in Nepal and has become the 'guardian' of the children there. Haven't even started the work, and the marketing to turn him into a god has already kicked off," his tweet read.
Sonu Sood hits back at criticism
The actor wasted no time responding to the criticism, writing back, "You are a good person, brother! Come to Nepal, both brothers will work together."
Sonu Sood shares update from flood site
On Thursday, Sonu took to X to share a video of himself walking through and inspecting the flood-hit areas, noting that the flood's impact was strong enough to reach even four-storey buildings. 
In another post carrying pictures from the site, he wrote, "Standing here today at the Trishuli River, where the floods have left behind unimaginable loss..broken homes, broken families, and lives changed forever. Nepal is not alone. I stand with its people, and I will do everything I can to bring hope, rebuild homes, and help families begin again."
Sonu Sood on relief efforts
Talking to ANI on Wednesday, Sonu said, "We are here to meet the victims of the flood. We got lots of stuff from India. We just want to be with the people who are in need and will try to bring their lives back (on track), I think it's everyone's duty to do their part. We have a lot of blankets and food materials. We are still asking them what they need; we try to send it from India. Sending from India to Nepal is always a little challenge because we need a lot of people. But we will make sure that not only this month but also in thecoming months, the relief keeps coming."
Sonu Sood's visit amid rising death toll
According to the latest update from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) issued on Thursday, the death toll from the flash floods has climbed to 1,252, with roughly 4,216 people still missing or unreachable. The authority also reported that about 11,993 people have been rescued so far, while 5,135 injured individuals have received medical care, of whom 301 were treated at hospitals, and the Nepali Army and Armed Police Force attended to 3,206 and 1,628 people, respectively.

title: Why Nepal is burying its flood victims instead of cremating them
text:
Nepal is a Hindu-majority country where cremation is the customary final rite for most Hindus. Yet after the devastating floods that swept through parts of the country, authorities have been burying unidentified bodies instead of cremating them. The reason is not a change in religious practice. It is a response to the large number of bodies being recovered, limited morgue space and the fact that many victims cannot yet be identified.
Authorities are treating the burials as a temporary arrangement. Before a body is placed in the ground, officials are collecting DNA samples and recording identifying details so that families may still be able to locate and claim the remains later.
According to The Statesman and various media reports, unidentified flood victims are being buried in Chitwan district after authorities collect DNA samples, assign identification codes and record the exact locations of their graves.
Why are the bodies being buried?
Bodies recovered from the floods were also beginning to decompose, making prolonged storage increasingly difficult.
The scale of the disastrous floods has put Nepal's mortuaries under severe pressure. Bodies recovered from the floods were also beginning to decompose, making prolonged storage increasingly difficult. 
According to media reports, authorities were dealing with unidentified bodies at hospitals while freezing facilities were unable to accommodate all the remains. With the bodies decomposing, temporary burial became necessary.
Morgues and mortuaries were overwhelmed by the number of bodies being brought in, leaving authorities with the difficult task of managing and preserving unidentified remains. The burials therefore do not mean that the victims' identities have been abandoned. Instead, authorities are trying to preserve enough information to identify them later.
Each body is being given an identification number
Each unidentified victim is assigned a unique identification code, while the burial location is recorded so the remains can be traced later.
The bodies are not simply being placed in an anonymous mass grave. Authorities are creating records for the individual remains. According to The Statesman, each unidentified victim is assigned a unique identification code, while the burial location is recorded so the remains can be traced later. This creates a link between the remains and the records kept by the authorities. The burial sites are also being documented. Photographs and other records are being maintained, while GPS coordinates are being recorded for the graves. That means authorities can potentially locate a particular grave even after the burial has taken place.
DNA is the key to identifying the dead
DNA samples are being collected from unidentified bodies before burial. At the same time, relatives of people reported missing can provide their own DNA samples. The samples can then be compared with DNA taken from the recovered remains. DNA records are being preserved specifically to allow future identification if relatives come forward.
The process is important because some bodies have been recovered far from where people went missing, while others are too badly decomposed or damaged to be identified through appearance alone.
Officials are recording more than genetic material. According to various media, photographs, clothing, jewellery, tattoos and other identifying marks are also being documented. Nepal Police has also published details of some unidentified victims in an effort to help families searching for missing relatives.
Why are the graves being prepared carefully?
The burial arrangement is designed with future identification in mind. Burial pits are being dug around 1.5 metres deep, with about 40 cm of space left between bodies. The arrangement is intended to reduce the risk of DNA contamination and make future identification and exhumation possible.
What happens if a victim is identified later?
Photo credit: Reuters
Identification does not end with the burial. If DNA testing establishes that a buried victim is the missing member of a family, officials can use the identification number and burial records to locate the remains. According to media reports, the remains can be handed over to the family once the victim has been identified. The family can then perform the funeral rites according to its traditions. This is why the burials are being handled differently from a conventional mass burial. Authorities are attempting to preserve the identity of every victim even when the person cannot be named immediately.
The problem is bigger than the burial grounds
The decision to bury the unidentified bodies comes as Nepal continues to deal with a large number of missing people. Close to a thousand bodies have been recovered and thousands of people are still missing.

title: Nepal flash floods: Relatives hold symbolic funerals for thousands missing as toll crosses 1,243
text:
The death toll from devastating flash floods in the Nepal-Tibet region rose to 1,243 on Thursday, as rescue teams battled heavy rain and thick debris while searching for people believed to be trapped in tunnels and underground power facilities along the Bhotekoshi River.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah said Nepal must raise the disasterâs connection to climate change with the international community, as families held symbolic funerals for relatives who remain missing following last weekâs floods.
Speaking at the fifth daily press briefing in Kathmandu, ministry of foreign affairs spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said authorities had begun conducting temporary burials for victims as search and rescue operations continued around the clock.
Chhetri said 11,993 people had been rescued, while 1,114 bodies had been recovered. Around 3,900 people remain unaccounted for, he said, urging relatives of those missing to provide DNA samples at the Nepal Police Hospital in Maharajgunj or their nearest District Police Office to help forensic teams with identification.
He also outlined international assistance being provided to Nepal. A 19-member forensic team from India is working with Nepal Police on DNA analysis, while specialised teams and equipment have also arrived from China, Singapore and South Korea to support identification and recovery efforts.
Rescue teams from the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force are working with international specialists from India, China and South Korea to clear mud, debris and boulders from underground hydropower facilities in areas including Langtang, Chilime and Upper Trisuli.
According to the ANI report, more than 300 foreign nationals have been safely rescued, while around 590 citizens from 34 countries remain unaccounted for.
Working with Chinese authorities, Nepal has also helped evacuate about 2,500 pilgrims returning from Mount Kailash through the Hilsa and Tatopani border crossings and via air routes through Lhasa. Efforts are also underway to clear stranded cargo and assist Nepali nationals near the Kerung border.
Addressing Parliament earlier Wednesday, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophic August 26 Bhotekoshi River floods, triggered by a high-altitude Himalayan avalanche, underscored the growing threat posed by climate change across the region.
Shah said nearly 4,000 people remain missing across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, stressing that addressing the effects of climate change requires a collective global effort.
As Nepal continues to coordinate international assistance from India, China, the United States, Japan, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank, the European Union and the United Nations, authorities are deploying available resources toward emergency relief, searches for missing people and long-term recovery.
According to Nepal Police, 348 bodies were recovered in Chitwan, 217 in Nawalparasi East, 190 in Nawalparasi West and 155 in Nuwakot. Another 66 bodies were recovered in Gorkha, 59 in Dhading, 45 in Rasuwa and 38 in Tanahu.
A total of 7,912 police personnel have been deployed to flood-hit areas to assist with search and rescue operations, distribute relief supplies and manage recovered bodies.
Authorities have also published details of 911 unidentified bodies on the Nepal Police website to help families identify missing relatives.
Meanwhile, rainwater accumulating inside a hydropower tunnel has created additional difficulties for search and rescue teams working in areas affected by the Bhotekoshi floods, said Dharma Raj Uprety, executive chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).
Search operations have been particularly challenging because of the hazardous conditions inside the projectâs tunnels. Teams from the Nepali Army and Armed Police Force, along with foreign technical experts and project employees, are continuing efforts to locate workers who remain missing.
As per the PTI report, Ganesh Karki, former president of the Independent Power Producersâ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), said rescue operations have also been slowed by difficulties transporting heavy equipment to the tunnels.

title: Miraculous rescue in Nepal: 1.5 month-old baby pulled to safety from flood-hit Rasuwa
text:
Amid the heartbreaking scenes coming out of flood-hit Nepal, one rescue has given people something to hold on to.
A 45-day-old baby was rescued from a flood-affected area in Rasuwa district and taken safely to the Rasuwa Dhange relief camp, according to reports on September 1.
The tiny infant was among those caught up in the flooding as rescue teams continued working through areas badly affected by floods and flash floods.
The rescue itself may have taken only moments, but the image of the baby being carried to safety has touched people following the disaster.
45-day-old baby rescued in Rasuwa
The rescue took place in Rasuwa, a district in northern Nepal that has been severely affected by flooding.
According to reports, the one-and-a-half-month-old baby was rescued from the affected area and brought to the Rasuwa Dhange camp.
Images and video from the rescue show the infant being carried by rescuers after being brought out of the danger zone.
And that small detail - 45 days old - is what makes the rescue especially emotional.
The baby is barely six weeks old.
At an age when a child should be sleeping safely at home, surrounded by family, the infant instead became part of a major emergency evacuation.
A moment of relief during a devastating disaster
Rasuwa has been hit by severe flooding and flash floods, leaving communities struggling with damaged homes, roads and other infrastructure.
Rescue teams have been working to reach stranded residents and move people to safer locations.
Against that backdrop, the safe evacuation of a newborn has offered a rare moment of relief.
There is no need to dress it up as anything more than that.
One tiny life was pulled out of a disaster zone and taken somewhere safer.
For families still waiting for news of their loved ones, moments like this matter.
The rescue video has touched people
Footage of the baby being brought to safety has circulated widely as news of the rescue spread.
The image is difficult to ignore.
A tiny infant is being carried through an area devastated by flooding, while rescue workers continue their efforts around them.
It's a striking reminder of how vulnerable people can become during a natural disaster - especially babies, children and elderly residents who cannot protect or move themselves.
But the footage also shows something else.
People were still out there searching.
Rescue operations continue
The baby's rescue came as emergency teams continued operations across flood-affected parts of Rasuwa and other areas of Nepal.
Rescuers have been working to locate stranded residents, evacuate families and provide assistance to people who have lost access to their homes.
The work has been difficult.
Floodwaters and damaged roads have made it harder to reach some communities, while rescue personnel have had to operate in dangerous conditions.
For those living in affected areas, getting to a safe place is often only the first step. Families also need food, shelter, medical assistance and basic supplies.
What is confirmed about the baby?
The central details are clear: a one-and-a-half-month-old, or roughly 45-day-old, baby was rescued from a flood-hit part of Rasuwa and taken safely to the Rasuwa Dhange camp.
Some social media posts may contain additional claims about the baby's condition or the exact circumstances of the rescue.
Those details should be treated carefully unless they are confirmed by authorities or reliable reporting.
What is known is that the infant was successfully rescued and brought to the relief camp.
And that, in itself, is significant.
One small rescue in the middle of a huge tragedy
It's tempting to call the rescue a miracle. But behind that moment were people who had to keep working through difficult conditions.
Someone had to reach the affected area. Someone had to find the baby. And someone had to carry that tiny child to safety. The infant couldn't understand what was happening. The child couldn't walk, run or escape. The rescuers had to do all of it. That's what makes the moment so powerful.
The floods have created a huge humanitarian challenge for Nepal, with communities dealing with destruction and families waiting for news of loved ones.
There are still difficult days ahead for many of those affected.
But in the middle of all that heartbreaking news, the rescue of a 45-day-old baby gives people one small reason to feel hopeful.
The baby was found.
The baby was brought out of danger.
And the baby reached Dhange camp safely.
Sometimes, during a disaster, one life saved is enough to remind everyone why the rescue effort matters.

title: UP floods: Rivers cross danger marks at 11 stations, over 11,000 hectares inundated
text:
LUCKNOW: Rivers in Uttar Pradesh reached or crossed danger levels at several monitoring stations as satellite data showed inundation of 11,358.49 hectares across five districts, highlighting the spread of flood conditions in the state.
The affected districts are Ballia, Ghazipur, Gorakhpur, Mau and Deoria.
The inundation figures were released by the Flood Management Information System Centre (FMISC) under the Uttar Pradesh irrigation department.
Its satellite-based assessment, prepared using RISAT-1A MRS SAR data analysed by the National Remote Sensing Centre, showed major inundation in Ballia and Ghazipur and minor inundation in Gorakhpur, Mau and Deoria by Monday evening.
UP inundated districts
Ballia reported flooding in 179 villages across 12 blocks, covering approximately 8,061.63 hectares. Ghazipur saw inundation in 87 villages across six blocks, covering 2,341.33 hectares.
Deoria reported flooding in 18 villages across five blocks, Gorakhpur in 14 villages across three blocks, and Mau in 13 villages in one block.
The combined assessment covered 311 villages in 27 blocks. The total submerged area was estimated at 11,358.49 hectares.
The FMISC clarified that the assessment includes riverine flooding, water accumulation in low-lying areas, rainfall-induced flooding and isolated waterlogged patches.
According to the Central Water Commissionâs readings available at 9 pm on Tuesday, water levels were at or above the danger mark at 11 monitoring stations in Uttar Pradesh.
The situation was serious along the Ganga, Ghaghra and their tributaries in Budaun, Barabanki, Ballia, Mirzapur, Varanasi and Ghazipur.
At Kachhla Bridge in Budaun, the Ganga was flowing at 162.43 m, exactly at the danger level. Its warning level is 161.80 m.
In Barabanki, the Ghaghra at Elginbridge was flowing at 106.09 m, 2 cm above its danger mark of 106.07 m and more than a metre above the warning level of 105.07 m.
The CWC forecast suggested that the river could rise further to 106.07 m by 9 am on Wednesday.
The Sharda also known as Mahakali river at Kukea in Lakhimpur Kheri rose to 139.81 m, marginally above its danger level of 139.8 m and well above the warning level of 138.8 m.
The Ghaghra was also above the danger mark at Turtipar in Ballia, where it stood at 64.08 m against a danger level of 64.01 m. The station recorded 22 mm rainfall during the day.
The forecast, however, indicated a fall to 64 m by Wednesday morning.
In Ballia, the Ganga was flowing at 59.37 m, nearly 1.75 m above its danger level of 57.615 m. The district accounted for the largest share of the inundated area recorded by the stateâs FMISC.
The most pronounced river-level exceedances in eastern Uttar Pradesh were recorded along the Ganga and its tributaries. At Tendui in Varanasi district, the Varuna was flowing at 71.35 m against a danger level of 70.21 m. The station recorded 43 mm rainfall.
At Saidpur in Ghazipur, the Ganga stood at 67.52 m against a danger level of 67.19 m. The station recorded 68 mm rainfall. At the Ghazipur monitoring station, the river was flowing at 63.33 m, exceeding the danger level of 63.105 m. The level was rising and was forecast to reach 63.47 m by 8 am on Wednesday. The station recorded 63 mm rainfall.
In Mirzapur, the Ganga was above the danger mark at Ahraura and Chunar. At Ahraura, the river stood at 74.75 m against a danger level of 74.30 m, though the trend was declining. At Chunar, it was flowing at 72.82 m against a danger level of 72.78 m.
At Narayanpur in Mirzapur, the Ganga was at 72.59 m, above the warning level of 71.41 metres but 21 cm below the danger mark of 72.41 m. The station recorded the highest rainfall among the locations shown in the CWC data, at 75.4 mm.
The CWC data also recorded a high level at Chausa in neighbouring Bihar, where the Karamnasa was flowing at 61.86 m against a danger level of 60.39 m. The reading is significant for the downstream flood situation in eastern Uttar Pradesh.
âThe readings suggest that flood pressure is spread across multiple river systems rather than being confined to one stretch. While some stations showed a declining trend, water levels at several locations remained above danger marks, leaving riverbank settlements, agricultural fields, roads and embankments vulnerable,â said an official source.
